newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia gets ready to launch space probe to Mars.
newsitem.headline: Russia gets ready to launch space probe to Mars.

text.p: Russia, following hard on the heels of the United States, will send a probe on a 100 million km (60 million mile) mission to Mars this weekend to find out more about the icy planet and look for signs of life.
A spokesman for the Russian Space Agency said on Friday that the launch of the Mars-96 mission was on schedule.
"The rocket with the probe has been brought into position at the launchpad and all essential preparation work is being carried out," Anatoly Tkachev said by telephone. "We hope it will happen."
The six-tonne probe will lift off from Kazakhstan's Baikonur cosmodrome at 11.40 p.m. Moscow time on Saturday (2040 GMT). It is due to reach Mars on September 12 next year.

The $64 million Russian mission is the second of three planned trips from Earth to Mars in just over a month. The U.S. launched one robot voyage to the Red Planet two weeks ago and a second mission will blast off on December 2.
All will check for signs of water on the far-away planet -- a key clue to whether there once was life on Mars.
"Maybe we can resolve one of the secrets of Mars, whether there can be organic elements there," Russian mission head Albert Galeyev told a news conference on Monday.

The Mars-96 mission is being launched two years behind schedule due to cash shortages in Russia's hard-pressed space sector. The six-tonne probe will carry 1.1 tonnes of scientific equipment from 20 European countries and the United States.

The cost constraints have not disappeared -- missions to Russia's orbiting Mir space station have been delayed on several occasions and the cosmonauts there have filled sewage system reserve containers -- and the Russian venture has no back-up facility if things go wrong.
The probe includes two dart-like penetrators designed to pierce the Martian soil and take samples from below ground level and beam information back to the orbiting probe.
One spike is equipped with a U.S.-made device to search for organic traces in Mars' soil.
The Russian-made penetrators and a tiny U.S.-designed six-wheeled rover will land several hundred km (miles) from each other to investigate as much of the surface of the planet as possible.
But cost constraints in the Russian space agency mean that, unlike for the U.S. probes, there will be no back-up if things with the Russian launch go wrong.
Yuri Milov, deputy head of the Russian space agency, said this week that Russia had spent 350 billion roubles ($64 million) over two years to prepare for the mission.
The U.S. one-tonne Global Surveyor replaced NASA's $1 billion Mars Observer probe, which spun out of control in 1993, days before it was due to enter orbit around Mars.
Surveyor has identical copies of five of the seven scientific instruments on its ill-fated predecessor.

Its sophisticated camera will see objects on the surface of the planet as small as a car from an altitude of 230 miles (370 km) and will map 99 percent of the planet during one Martian year -- or 687 Earth days.
